news.content_title: Mpox cases in SA have climbed to 26
news.content: Twenty of this year’s 26 confirmed mpox cases came after August, concentrated mostly within the Western Cape. Elri Voigt looks at how the virus has changed and how much of the donated vaccine is left. The viral illness mpox has caused several clusters of outbreaks across the world. In South Africa, sporadic cases have been detected, but an uptick since August has now brought the illness back into the spotlight. As of 27 October, 26 mpox cases have been confirmed in South Africa this year, Dr Jacqueline Weyer, Head of the Centre for Emerging Zoonotic and Parasitic Diseases at the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD), told Spotlight. Of those 26 cases , 18 are in the Western Cape, three are in Gauteng, two are in the Eastern Cape, another two are in the Free State and one is in KwaZulu-Natal. The majority of cases, 20, have been detected since August this year. All but one of these cases were in men between the ages of 23 and 50 years. One case was in a woman aged 35 to 44. Seven people have been admitted to hospital , but no deaths have been reported so far this year. Mpox was first identified in humans in 1970, and was mostly observed in Central, East and West Africa . The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) was particularly affected, with thousands of cases reported since 2005. Then in 2022, the virus spread rapidly to multiple countries for the first time. About 140 countries have reported mpox cases since 2022, according to the World Health Organization’s mpox dashboard , with more than 190,000 laboratory-confirmed cases reported and over 536 deaths to date. The overall number of mpox cases in South Africa has been low. Our back-of-the-envelope calculation puts the total confirmed number of mpox cases since 2022 at 71. The NICD mpox dashboard lists a total of 66 cases and three deaths between 2024 and 2026 . In 2023, according to Weyer, there were no reported cases of mpox in the country. There were five cases of mpox identified in 2022, according to information on the NICD’s page on mpox . While the number of mpox cases have been relatively low to date, the current situation can be referred to as an outbreak. Weyer told Spotlight an “outbreak” doesn’t necessarily mean a “large number” of people are affected. “Outbreaks may be large, small and confined, and for some conditions, a single case may be denoted as an outbreak.” In public health, she added, an outbreak “refers to the occurrence of cases of a disease in a particular place and period that warrants investigation and a public health response”. When asked if there is a risk for a larger mpox outbreak in the country, Weyer is cautious. “ We cannot rule out the possibility of further cases, particularly while investigations are ongoing and local transmission has occurred previously,” she said. “The risk of further spread depends on several factors, including how quickly cases are detected, the number and nature of contacts, the extent of transmission within affected networks, and the effectiveness of public health measures.” She added: “We have the opportunity to intervene early, identify additional cases and reduce the likelihood of further spread.” She said the NICD’s approach is to remain alert without creating unnecessary alarm. “We are continuing to strengthen surveillance, laboratory investigation, contact tracing, vaccination of eligible priority groups and public awareness,” she said. There is a limited number of donated mpox vaccines available in South Africa. Since there are currently no registered vaccines against mpox or other treatment options in the country, any vaccine or treatment used will need to be supplied via a Section 21 request, which allows for medicines that are not registered in South Africa to be brought in. Vaccines against smallpox – which is caused by a virus closely related to the mpox virus – can offer some protection against the illness. There are three vaccines that can be used against mpox – LC16m8, MVA-BN and ACAM2000 . The latter is only registered for limited use in the United States. Last year, the Africa Centres for Disease control and Prevention (Africa CDC) donated just over 10,000 doses of the vaccine MVA-BN (known by the brand names imvanex and JYNNEOS) to the national Department of Health. These doses have been used in vaccination efforts ever since, with a total of 2,365 doses administered between September 2025 and September 2026, health department spokesperson Foster Mohale told Spotlight. There are currently 3,865 doses still available for use, according to Mohale, which will expire on 31 August 2027. We asked the health department about the remaining 4,000 or so doses but are still awaiting a reply. When asked whether any additional mpox vaccines would be procured or donated, Mohale said: “Yes, the department is currently reviewing procurement options of additional mpox vaccine doses, dependent on the recommendation from [the] Incident Management Team and the National Advisory Group on Immunisation.” Mohale said vaccine doses are distributed to provinces as required, depending on “disease outbreak and response”. Vaccination for mpox is recommended for people who are at high risk of acquiring the virus and at risk of getting severe disease. It can also be considered as a form of post-exposure prophylaxis for people who have been in contact with someone who has mpox. An antiviral medicine called tecovirimat is occasionally used to treat mpox symptoms in severe cases. There is some limited stock of the drug available for use in South Africa, which Mohale said was sourced through the World Health Organization (WHO) and Africa CDC’s Access and Allocation Mechanism. There are still more than 40 containers of tecovirimat capsules available, Mohale said. But there are not currently any plans to procure more, although he added that this will be dependent on the recommendation from the Incident Management Team and the National Essential Medicines List Committee. He did not say how many treatment courses are in a container. In a 2025 national Department of Health mpox guideline document , the National Essential Medicines List Committee suggests that tecovirimat should only be used to treat those with severe disease who have been admitted to hospital. This is because the drug has not been shown to make any significant difference in most cases of mpox. Earlier this year, results from a phase 3 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine showed that there was “no evidence that tecovirimat therapy shortened the time to clinical resolution, reduced pain, or increased viral clearance among adults with clade II mpox”. At first, mpox cases in the country were traced back to international travel. Then in 2024 and 2025 we started seeing local transmission. Most people diagnosed with mpox in 2024 reported no recent international travel history, Weyer said, noting that “the epidemiological assessment indicated that local person-to-person transmission was occurring”. For the current situation, Weyer said local transmission is “implied”, noting that investigations are still ongoing. “This has been established by identifying contact links between cases, and identifying the same clade and sub-lineage of the mpox virus associated with the cases to date.” There were some individuals who were diagnosed with mpox this year who had recently been out of the country. One of the people had recently travelled to Spain , while another had travelled to Belgium. In two other cases international travellers came to South Africa already carrying the virus. The mpox virus has two clades, clade I and clade II, with several sub-clades. Professor Tulio de Oliveira, Director of the Centre for Epidemic Response and Innovation at Stellenbosch University, explained to Spotlight previously that clades are a classification system based on the genetic similarities between different strains of a virus. “So, what it means is that when we see a genetic change [in a virus] that’s really visible and that may have impacted it, normally we call it a different clade or genotype or variant,” he said at the time. For now, the two mpox sub-clades that are driving most cases in people are sub-clade Ib and sub-clade IIb. This year, cases of mpox in South Africa are a mix of the two sub-clades. The mpox dashboard shows that of the 26 cases , 19 were sub-clade Ib, four were sub-clade IIb, and three cases didn’t have sub-clade information available. In 2022, sub-clade IIb was driving the mpox outbreak, said Weyer. This changed by 2024 when a new strain of the mpox virus spread beyond the DRC. Sub-clade Ib was first identified in the DRC in 2023 and was behind a large outbreak of the illness in the country that year. This sub-clade spread from the DRC through international travel, and cases of sub- clade Ib were reported across the globe by 2024 . The first case of mpox where sequencing indicated sub-clade Ib in South Africa was detected in 2025, according to the NICD dashboard. A total of 15 mpox cases were reported that year, and sequencing information was available in all but one of the cases. Weyer said that at the moment there is not any evidence to indicate that there are additional mpox clades or sub-clades circulating in the country. Knowing which clade or sub-clade someone with mpox has doesn’t change how their illness is managed. Instead, it helps scientists track outbreaks. “Understanding the genetic character of the viruses assists us in tracking outbreaks, evolution of the viruses and identifying markers which may affect diagnostic test performance and potentially vaccine efficacy,” Weyer said. “The central priorities remain early diagnosis, appropriate clinical care, identifying and monitoring contacts, vaccination of eligible target groups, and communicating accurate information without stigmatising affected individuals or communities. The approach is the same regardless of the current genetic character of these viruses,” she added. Mpox is mainly spread through close contact with someone who has the virus or contact with material like bedding or clothing that has been in contact with someone with mpox. The illness can cause flu-like symptoms – like a headache, sore throat, fever and muscle aches – as well as a distinct and often painful rash. The rash can occur on someone’s palms or soles of their feet, face, mouth and throat and sometimes the genital areas. It starts as a flat sore, then becomes a blister which can be itchy or painful. As the rash heals, the lesions dry up, crust over and fall off. The virus has an incubation period of anything from five to 21 days – but usually it is around seven to 14 days. “Mpox can affect anyone who has close contact with an infected person. We should avoid assumptions about who can acquire the infection and ensure that people feel able to seek healthcare without fear of judgement or discrimination,” said Weyer. Mpox is normally diagnosed by swabbing the lesions from the rash and sending that for testing with a PCR (polymerase chain reaction) test that looks for the virus’ DNA. While the overall case fatality for mpox is low, typically below 1% , people who are immunocompromised (such as people living with uncontrolled HIV), pregnant women, and children, have a much higher risk of severe illness, complications and even death. In most cases, according to the mpox guideline document, symptoms can be managed at home, with rash-related pain being a particular challenge. Severe mpox cases require being admitted to hospital. Someone who has mpox is considered contagious until the rash has completely gone away, and the scabs have healed . Thus, people diagnosed with mpox are advised to self-isolate until their rash has gone away completely. “People who develop an unexplained rash, particularly when accompanied by fever, swollen lymph nodes or a history of possible exposure, should seek medical assessment,” Weyer advised. “They should avoid close physical contact with others while awaiting clinical guidance and testing. The public should understand that mpox is preventable and that early diagnosis and appropriate care are important in reducing transmission and complications.” DM This article was first published by Spotlight – health journalism in the public interest. news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 9, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology First Mpox Genomes from Uruguay Reveal Multiple Introductions and Limited Spread by November 6, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 First Mpox Genomes from Uruguay Reveal Multiple Introductions and Limited Spread Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers have generated and analyzed the first 17 monkeypox virus genomes from Uruguay, resolving a lack of publicly available genomic data from the 2022 global clade IIb epidemic. According to a brief report published in Virology Journal, Uruguay experienced a limited mpox outbreak during the global epidemic. The 17 newly sequenced viral genomes were sampled during the 2022 outbreak and represent approximately 85 percent of the 20 confirmed national cases reported as of 2025. By integrating phylogenetic inferences with patient travel history and contact-tracing data, the investigation identified evidence of up to eight independent viral introductions into the country. These introduction events involved monkeypox virus lineages B.1, B.1.2, and B.1.6. Genomic and epidemiological tracing linked the introductions to travel from Brazil, Argentina, and Chile, establishing that the pathogen arrived through multiple cross-border events. Despite these repeated introductions, the study determined that local transmission chains within Uruguay remained short and geographically restricted. These findings indicate that the small scale of Uruguay’s outbreak was driven not by fewer viral introductions, but by limited onward transmission. As the first genomic characterization of mpox in Uruguay, the research demonstrates the importance of combining genomic surveillance with epidemiological investigations during emerging outbreaks. analysis.time: The study was conducted during the 2022 mpox outbreak, with the publication date on November 6, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: Uruguay, with the outbreak affecting approximately 20 confirmed national cases as of 2025.
analysis.event: Researchers sequenced and analyzed the first 17 monkeypox virus genomes from Uruguay, revealing multiple introductions and limited local spread during the 2022 global clade IIb epidemic. This was reported by Bioengineer.org.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study found evidence of up to eight independent viral introductions, but local transmission chains remained short and geographically restricted. The small scale of the outbreak was attributed to limited onward transmission rather than fewer introductions.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The investigation integrated genomic data with patient travel history and contact-tracing data to identify the introductions. The findings are based on genomic surveillance and epidemiological investigations, and the study is considered complete with no unresolved information.

analysis.brief_en: Researchers in Uruguay have sequenced and analyzed the first 17 monkeypox virus genomes from the 2022 global clade IIb epidemic, revealing multiple independent introductions of the virus into the country. These introductions were linked to travel from Brazil, Argentina, and Chile, with the virus lineages B.1, B.1.2, and B.1.6 identified. Despite these repeated introductions, local transmission chains were found to be short and geographically restricted, indicating that the limited spread of the outbreak was due to restricted transmission rather than fewer viral entries. The study, published in Virology Journal, highlights the importance of combining genomic surveillance with epidemiological data during emerging outbreaks. The research was conducted by a team of scientists and published on November 6, 2026, by Bioengineer.org, providing a comprehensive understanding of the outbreak dynamics in Uruguay.
analysis.summary_en: Researchers in Uruguay have sequenced and analyzed the first 17 monkeypox virus genomes from the 2022 global clade IIb epidemic, revealing multiple independent introductions of the virus into the country. These introductions were linked to travel from Brazil, Argentina, and Chile, with the virus lineages B.1, B.1.2, and B.1.6 identified. Despite these repeated introductions, local transmission chains were found to be short and geographically restricted, indicating that the limited spread of the outbreak was due to restricted transmission rather than fewer viral entries. The study, published in Virology Journal, highlights the importance of combining genomic surveillance with epidemiological data during emerging outbreaks. The research was conducted by a team of scientists and published on November 6, 2026, by Bioengineer.org, providing a comprehensive understanding of the outbreak dynamics in Uruguay.

news.title_zh: 乌拉圭首次发现猴痘 基因组揭示多次引入和有限传播 - Bioengineer.org
news.source_body_en: Researchers in Uruguay have sequenced and analyzed the first 17 monkeypox virus genomes from the 2022 global clade IIb epidemic, revealing multiple independent introductions of the virus into the country. These introductions were linked to travel from Brazil, Argentina, and Chile, with the virus lineages B.1, B.1.2, and B.1.6 identified. Despite these repeated introductions, local transmission chains were found to be short and geographically restricted, indicating that the limited spread of the outbreak was due to restricted transmission rather than fewer viral entries. The study, published in Virology Journal, highlights the importance of combining genomic surveillance with epidemiological data during emerging outbreaks. The research was conducted by a team of scientists and published on November 6, 2026, by Bioengineer.org, providing a comprehensive understanding of the outbreak dynamics in Uruguay.
news.content_zh: 乌拉圭研究人员对2022年全球IIb谱系疫情中首次发现的17例猴痘病毒基因组进行了测序和分析,揭示了该病毒多次独立传入该国。这些传入与来自巴西、阿根廷和智利的旅行有关,并鉴定出病毒谱系B.1、B.1.2和B.1.6。尽管有这些重复传入,但本地传播传播链被发现较短且地理上受限,表明该病毒在乌拉圭的有限传播是由于传播受限,而非病毒传入次数较少。该研究发表于《病毒学杂志》,强调在新兴暴发期间结合基因组监测与流行病学数据的重要性。该研究由一组科学家进行,并于2026年11月6日由Bioengineer.org发布,提供了对乌拉圭暴发动态的全面理解。
news.summary_zh: 乌拉圭研究人员对2022年全球IIb谱系疫情中首次发现的17例猴痘病毒基因组进行了测序和分析,揭示了该病毒多次独立传入该国。这些传入与来自巴西、阿根廷和智利的旅行有关,并鉴定出病毒谱系B.1、B.1.2和B.1.6。尽管有这些重复传入,但本地传播传播链被发现较短且地理上受限,表明该病毒在乌拉圭的有限传播是由于传播受限,而非病毒传入次数较少。该研究发表于《病毒学杂志》,强调在新兴暴发期间结合基因组监测与流行病学数据的重要性。该研究由一组科学家进行,并于2026年11月6日由Bioengineer.org发布,提供了对乌拉圭暴发动态的全面理解。

analysis_zh.time: 该研究是在2022年猴痘 暴发期间进行的,发表日期为2026年11月6日。
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 乌拉圭,截至2025年,该国约有20例确认的暴发病例。
analysis_zh.event: 乌拉圭研究人员对首次发现的17例猴痘病毒基因组进行了测序和分析,揭示了在2022年全球IIb谱系疫情期间该病毒的多次传入和有限本地传播。此结果由Bioengineer.org报道。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 研究发现有最多八次独立的病毒传入,但本地传播传播链仍较短且地理上受限。该病毒传播规模较小的原因归因于传播受限,而非传入次数较少。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 该调查结合了基因组数据、患者旅行史和接触追踪数据以确定病毒传入情况。研究结果基于基因组监测和流行病学调查,且研究被认为已完整,没有未解决的信息。

news.wechat_summary_zh: 时间：该研究是在2022年猴痘 暴发期间进行的，发表日期为2026年11月6日。；地点与对象：乌拉圭，截至2025年，该国约有20例确认的暴发病例。；事件：乌拉圭研究人员对首次发现的17例猴痘病毒基因组进行了测序和分析，揭示了在2022年全球IIb谱系疫情期间该病毒的多次传入和有限本地传播。此结果由Bioengineer.org报道。；影响与风险：研究发现有最多八次独立的病毒传入，但本地传播传播链仍较短且地理上受限。该病毒传播规模较小的原因归因于传播受限，而非传入次数较少。；应对与不确定性：该调查结合了基因组数据、患者旅行史和接触追踪数据以确定病毒传入情况。研究结果基于基因组监测和流行病学调查，且研究被认为已完整，没有未解决的信息。

Send Close Sexually Transmitted Infections Share on Facebook Share on LinkedIn Share on X Email Article Copy Article Url Print NOVEMBER 8, 2026 U.S. Mpox Transmission Persists, but Vaccination Linked to Lower Hospitalization Risk By Ethan Covey Mpox continued to circulate at low levels in the United States during 2024 and 2025, with surveillance findings suggesting a possible transition toward endemic transmission of clade IIb mpox virus (MPXV) (MMWR Morb Mortal Wkly Rep 2026;75[32]:406-412). Vaccination can help prevent mpox. Source: Adobe. In order to study transmission patterns, investigators analyzed national surveillance data for 5,322 reported MPXV infections, including 2,803 cases in 2024 and 2,519 in 2025. Cases increased during fall 2025, with 873 reported during September and October, approximately double the 423 cases reported during the same period in 2024. Case counts returned to background levels by the end of December 2025. Demographic patterns were generally similar to those of previous years. Most cases occurred among men; among men who reported sexual orientation, 79% identified as gay or bisexual. Black and Hispanic patients were disproportionately affected relative to their representation in the men who have sex with men and overall U.S. populations. Vaccination status was available for 2,049 patients. Among those, 76.1% were unvaccinated, 14.3% were fully vaccinated with two doses of JYNNEOS (Bavarian Nordic), and 9.6% were partially vaccinated. Among 860 patients with complete data, unvaccinated patients had 9.73 times the odds of hospitalization compared with fully vaccinated patients after adjustment for age group and HIV status. People living with HIV had 2.37 times the odds of hospitalization compared with those without HIV. Eleven clade Ib cases were reported during 2024 and 2025, but investigators found no evidence of sustained transmission. Three patients with clade Ib infection were hospitalized, and no deaths were reported. “Continued circulation of clade IIb MPXV in the U.S. since 2022 suggests a transition toward endemicity,” the authors of the report wrote. In order to reduce the risk for mpox transmission, the CDC recommends continued surveillance and that people at risk for MPXV exposure complete the recommended two-dose JYNNEOS vaccination series. The study authors reported no relevant financial disclosures. news.wechat_summary_zh: 时间：该研究分析了2024年和2025年的数据，病例数量在2025年12月底恢复到背景水平。本文于2026年11月8日发表。；地点与对象：美国，重点关注男性同性性行为者，尤其是自我认同为同性恋或双性恋的男性，以及受影响更为严重的黑人和西班牙裔患者。；事件：猴痘病毒在美国2024年和2025年持续以低水平传播，监测结果表明可能向IIb簇猴痘病毒的本地流行转变。；影响与风险：共分析了5，322例报告的猴痘病毒感染病例，其中2024年为2，803例，2025年为2，519例。2025年秋季病例数量增加，9月和10月报告了873例，是2024年同期423例的两倍。在860例有完整数据...；应对与不确定性：CDC建议继续监测，并建议有猴痘病毒暴露风险的人群完成推荐的两剂JYNNEOS疫苗接种系列。研究作者报告称没有相关的财务披露。

news.content: Menu SECTIONS News Features CME/CE Clinical Tools Conferences Special Collections Multimedia DermDx OrthoDx Clinical Challenge Advisor Forum Fact Sheets Legal Advisor Submit a Manuscript Topics Allergy and Immunology Cardiovascular Cases Dermatology Diabetes Diet and Nutrition Endocrinology Gastroenterology General Medicine Geriatrics Hematology Infectious Disease Legal Advisor Men’s Health Nephrology Neurology Ob/GYN Obesity Oncology Opinion Orthopedics Pain Pediatrics Practice Management Psychiatry Pulmonology Rheumatology Surgery Urology Women’s Health Haymarket Medical Network Cancer Therapy Advisor Cardiology Advisor Clinical Advisor Clinical Pain Advisor Dermatology Advisor Endocrinology Advisor Gastroenterology Advisor Hematology Advisor Infectious Disease Advisor Medical Bag MPR Neurology Advisor Obesity Advisor Oncology Nurse Advisor Ophthalmology Advisor Optometry Advisor Psychiatry Advisor Pulmonology Advisor Rare Disease Advisor Renal and Urology News Rheumatology Advisor Sleep Wake Advisor Vaccine Advisor Search for: News CME/CE Features Opinion Advisor Forum Meetings Resources Drug info Part of the News and Features CME/CE Conferences Clinical Tools Special Collections Multimedia Share this article Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Bluesky Share by Email Print Nonsexually Acquired Mpox Associated With Higher Hospitalization Rates Hibah Khaja, PharmD | Publish Date November 3, 2026 Researchers evaluated demographic and clinical differences between patients with sexually and nonsexually acquired clade II mpox in California. Compared with sexual transmission, nonsexually acquired clade II mpox is associated with an increased risk for hospitalization, a higher prevalence of HIV, and lower vaccination rates. Patients with clade II mpox (previously monkeypox) resulting from nonsexual transmission are more frequently hospitalized and have a higher prevalence of HIV than those who report recent sexual contact, according to study results presented at IDWeek 2026, held from October 21 to 24, in Washington, DC. Researchers evaluated differences in demographic characteristics, clinical outcomes, and potential exposures among patients with sexually and nonsexually acquired mpox in California. The analysis included confirmed and probable clade II mpox cases reported to the California Department of Public Health between May 2022 and December 2024. Drawing on public health surveillance records, the researchers sorted cases into groups based on whether patients reported sexual activity in the 21 days before their symptoms began. Patients who denied sexual contact during this period were included in the nonsexual exposure group only if their initial lesions occurred outside the genital and perianal regions. Those reporting no sexual contact but presenting with lesions initially involving these areas were excluded from that group. More information is needed on the dynamics of which populations may be at risk for non-sexual mpox transmission for targeted messaging and strategies. Demographic and clinical characteristics were compared using proportions via the Wilson method. Statistical significance was assessed based on whether the CIs overlapped between groups. Of 6651 reported mpox cases, 5206 had sufficient information to determine sexual exposure classification. Among these patients, 561 (10.8%) were categorized as having nonsexually acquired mpox, while 4645 (89.2%) reported recent sexual contact. Hospitalization occurred in 12.5% of patients in the nonsexual exposure group compared with 4.7% in the sexual exposure group. The prevalence of HIV was also higher among patients classified as having nonsexually acquired mpox (53.3% vs 39.8%). The researchers reported differences in vaccination history and potential environmental exposure. Most patients in both groups were unvaccinated against mpox, although the proportion was higher among those in the nonsexual group (96.8% vs 87.9%). Receipt of 1 vaccine dose was reported in 2.3% vs 5.6% of patients, respectively, while 0.9% vs 6.5% had received 2 doses. Possible exposure through contaminated objects or surfaces was reported by 16.4% of patients in the nonsexual group compared with 10.0% of those in the sexual exposure group. Patients classified as having nonsexually acquired mpox also differed by age, sex at birth, and race and ethnicity. The proportion assigned female at birth was higher in the nonsexual group (4.6% vs 2.2%), as was the proportion younger than 18 years (2.3% vs 0.3%). Black patients accounted for 17.5% of nonsexual cases and 10.8% of sexual cases, while Hispanic or Latino patients represented 53.5% and 43.5%, respectively. White patients accounted for a smaller proportion of the nonsexual group than the sexual exposure group (18.5% vs 32.2%). Regarding sexual orientation, 20.0% of patients in the nonsexual group identified as heterosexual compared with 7.3% of those in the sexual exposure group. Conversely, 54.2% vs 73.7% identified as gay, lesbian, or same-gender loving. Patients declining to disclose their sexual orientation represented 5.9% and 5.4% of the respective groups. Geographic socioeconomic differences were identified using the Health Performance Index (HPI). Residence in an area within the lowest HPI quartile was more common among patients in the nonsexual group (38.5% vs 23.4%), whereas residence in the highest quartile was less common (14.5% vs 27.9%). All reported differences were considered statistically significant based on nonoverlapping 95% CIs. “More information is needed on the dynamics of which populations may be at risk for non-sexual mpox transmission for targeted messaging and strategies,” the researchers concluded. This article originally appeared on Infectious Disease Advisor References: Keinde A, Saadeh K, Tang EC, et al. Beyond sexual transmission: distinct demographic and clinical profiles of non-sexually acquired clade II mpox cases in California, May 2022-December 2024. Abstract presented at: IDWeek 2026; October 21-24; Washington, DC. Poster P-240

analysis.location_and_population: The study focused on California, specifically on patients with clade II mpox, comparing those with nonsexual transmission to those with sexual transmission.
analysis.event: Researchers evaluated demographic and clinical differences between patients with sexually and nonsexually acquired clade II mpox in California, finding that nonsexually acquired cases were associated with higher hospitalization rates, higher HIV prevalence, and lower vaccination rates.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Of 6651 reported mpox cases, 5206 had sufficient information for sexual exposure classification. 561 (10.8%) were categorized as nonsexually acquired, with 12.5% hospitalized compared to 4.7% in the sexual exposure group. HIV prevalence was 53.3% vs 39.8%, and vaccination rates were lower in the nonsexual group (96.8% unvaccinated vs 87.9% in the sexual group).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was presented at IDWeek 2026, and all reported differences were considered statistically significant based on nonoverlapping 95% CIs. The researchers concluded that more information is needed on non-sexual mpox transmission dynamics for targeted strategies.

analysis.brief_en: A study published on November 3, 2026, analyzed mpox cases in California between May 2022 and December 2024, comparing those with nonsexual transmission to those with sexual transmission. The research found that nonsexually acquired clade II mpox was associated with higher hospitalization rates (12.5% vs 4.7%), a higher prevalence of HIV (53.3% vs 39.8%), and lower vaccination rates (96.8% unvaccinated vs 87.9%). The study, presented at IDWeek 2026, included 6651 reported cases, with 5206 having sufficient data for sexual exposure classification. Of these, 561 (10.8%) were categorized as nonsexually acquired. news.title: New outbreak of mpox in Anchorage prompts advisory from state health officials
news.excerpt: The contagious disease, which was a problem during a global outbreak in 2022, is emerging again around the nation.

news.content_title: New outbreak of mpox in Anchorage prompts advisory from state health officials
news.content: FILE - This colorized electron microscope image provided by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases in 2024 shows mpox virus particles, green, found within infected cultured cells, blue. The virus particles are in various stages of maturity, which accounts for differences in shape. (NIAID via AP, File) A rare viral disease has emerged in an outbreak in Alaska’s largest city that appears to be expanding, state health officials report. There are now four new cases in Anchorage of mpox , a viral disease formerly called monkeypox that is spread through close contact and can be fatal. None of the patients reported traveling outside the state in the monthlong period before becoming infected. It is the highest number of annual mpox cases in Alaska since 2022, when five cases were diagnosed in the state amid a global outbreak . Between 2023 and 2025, there were only two Alaska cases. Three of the Anchorage cases emerged in October and were reported in late October through a state Department of Health alert intended to raise awareness in the public and among healthcare providers. The fourth case was reported to state officials Thursday, said Dr. Joe McLaughlin, Alaska’s state epidemiologist. The four Anchorage cases are among men who reported no travel outside of Alaska in the past 30 days, Mclaughlin said. That is a contrast with the previous Alaska cases, all of which were among people who had recent travel experiences. Up to now, travel had been implicated in the spread of mpox in Alaska. Officials are currently trying to track the source of infection, said McLaughlin and Dr. Randi Rollins, a U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention epidemiologist working with the Alaska Department of Health. The lack of reported out-of-state travel “does not necessarily establish that the monkeypox virus is circulating here in Alaska,” Rollins said. “They may have had exposure to somebody who traveled to Alaska, and they may be the end of that transmission line at this point. We don’t know.” Mpox is characterized by lesions that appear on various parts of the body. It usually takes three to 17 days after infection for symptoms to emerge, Rollins said, and in the first phase, the symptoms are flu-like: “fever, chills, fatigue, headache, sore muscles, and even swollen lymph nodes.” The lesions develop in the second phase, with bumps that are firm to the touch or sometimes tender, she said. Some people skip the early symptoms and do not have any signs of infection until the rash phase develops, she said. The sickness lasts a few weeks, and patients are considered to have recovered when all the lesions are gone. Until that last lesion is completely healed, “the person is still infectious and can transmit monkeypox, and that can typically take two to four weeks,” she said. McLaughlin said the Alaska patients are isolating and recovering. Two of the reported cases were among men who are partners, but it is unknown whether there are any additional links between any of the patients, he said. Increase in cases nationally The new outbreak of mpox in Anchorage fits a national pattern. After a lull that followed the 2022-23 global outbreak, cases are on the rise again in the United States. An uptick in infections started in March, the CDC reported. The virus circulating now is genetically different from the variety behind the global outbreak in 2022, which is called clade II. The currently circulating virus is called clade I. In Central Africa, the clade I variation had been more deadly than the clade II variation. But the current variation of the clade I virus appears to be not particularly deadly, according to health officials. Spread of the virus happens through close contact, including but not limited to sexual contact. Alaska health officials are encouraging anyone considered to be at risk of infection to get vaccinated. The JYNNEOS vaccine , approved by the Food and Drug Administration in 2019, guards against both clades of mpox, as well as smallpox, a disease that historically killed much of the world’s population but is now considered to have been eradicated. The vaccine, which is administered in two doses, is available through the Anchorage Health Department and other health providers. It is recommended for certain groups of people considered to be at higher risk for infections. Those include men who have sex with other men, anyone with exposure to another person suspected of having mpox, people who are traveling to parts of the world with mpox outbreaks and medical workers, such as those employed in labs or healthcare facilities, whose jobs put them at risk of being exposed to this and other pathogens. The vaccine is effective even for people already infected with the virus, reducing risks even for those who might develop the disease, Rollins said. For anyone who has been exposed, “it’s recommended that you get that vaccine within four days of exposure,” she said. While that time window is ideal, “you can get it up to about 14 days and still see effectiveness at reducing disease severity,” she said. State immunization records show that since 2022, 851 people in Alaska have received a first dose of the JYNNEOS vaccine and 604 receiving a second dose, Rollins said. A health professional shows doses of mpox vaccines at the Edison municipal vaccination center in Paris on July 27, 2022. The (Alain Jocard, Pool via AP, File) New borealpox cases reported While healthcare providers are being advised to watch for the resurgence of mpox, there is news about a rarer type of pox disease: borealpox. Two cases of borealpox , formerly known as Alaskapox, have been diagnosed this year, Rollins and McLaughlin said. That brings the world’s total number of diagnosed borealpox cases to nine. The disease, related to mpox, smallpox and other poxes, was first identified in 2015 in Fairbanks. The first six cases were found in Fairbanks and were considered to be mild. Like other pox diseases, they were characterized by skin lesions and some flu-like symptoms. However, in January of 2024, a Kenai Peninsula man died from borealpox after being infected by what scientists discovered was a genetically different strain of the virus. The patient was in his 60s and had an immune system weakened by treatment for cancer. This year’s two borealpox cases, like the previous Fairbanks-area cases, were mild, Rollins said. “It was the lesion that came to the attention of both patients, and they sought treatment for the lesion,” she said. “One patient did experience respiratory illness, fever, muscle aches, joint aches.” Scientists say borealpox circulates among small mammals . So far, red-backed voles, which are plentiful across most of Alaska, have been identified as a major source. Investigation of cases so far has focused on household pets that appear to have encountered infected voles or other small mammals. Unlike the case with mpox, there is no vaccine for borealpox. But some scientists are working on developing one, and some are investigating the effectiveness of certain antiviral medicines to treat infections. Originally published by the Alaska Beacon , an independent, nonpartisan news organization that covers Alaska state government

It is the highest number of annual mpox cases in Alaska since 2022, when five cases were diagnosed in the state amid a global outbreak . Between 2023 and 2025, there were only two Alaska cases.

The researchers mapped and synthesised existing published literature on vaccines as well as non-pharmaceutical preventive measures directed at mpox in pregnant women and paediatric populations. Their investigation aimed to assess reported vaccine effectiveness and to systematically identify the critical implementation barriers and facilitators influencing real-world prevention efforts across affected healthcare settings. To conduct the synthesis, the authors executed comprehensive searches across peer-reviewed and grey literature indexed in PubMed, Scopus, and Google for records published since 2008. The team completed their final database searches on 19 September 2025. Screening and data extraction followed a pre-specified review protocol structured in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews framework. Across the evaluated literature, forty-eight peer-reviewed articles and sixteen grey literature sources met the inclusion criteria, contributing evidence on immunisation strategies, preventive measures, documented effectiveness, implementation barriers, and delivery facilitators. Discover more health Health Academic research tools Within the identified literature, third-generation non-replicating vaccines, including MVA-BN, JYNNEOS, Imvanex, and IMVAMUNE, were consistently recommended for use in pregnant women and children owing to their favourable safety profiles. However, the scoping review revealed that documented observational and programmatic estimates of vaccine effectiveness were derived almost entirely from adult study populations. Reported effectiveness stood at 36 to 86 percent for a single dose and reached up to approximately 89 percent following two doses. Crucially, the review identified no effectiveness estimate specific to pregnant women or children. The authors also found that no source reported vaccine use by pregnancy trimester, paediatric data remained restricted to small studies, and recommendations for ring vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis were supported mainly by adult evidence. Discover more Engineering job board Research publication platform Scientific instrument sales Laboratory equipment supplier The review identified substantial implementation barriers that restrict mpox prevention and immunisation activities. Significant supply limitations and severe cold-chain and logistical constraints continue to impede vaccine rollout in low- and middle-income countries. In addition, vaccine hesitancy represents a major obstacle, largely driven by safety concerns that become particularly pronounced during pregnancy. These concerns are further intensified by the total absence of randomised controlled clinical trials conducted in pregnant women and paediatric groups. The authors also observed that geographic representation was severely skewed, noting that very few identified sources were centred on Africa or other low- and middle-income nations. Alongside these challenges, the scoping review documented key facilitators that have supported vaccination programs, such as international coordination, targeted surveillance initiatives, and the strategic integration of immunisation into routine maternal and child health services. The authors also highlighted flexible delivery strategies, specifically intradermal dosing, as mechanisms that can assist implementation under constrained resources. Looking ahead, the review outlined clear public health priorities, emphasising the urgent necessity of conducting prospective safety and immunogenicity studies in pregnancy and childhood, securing equitable vaccine access for low- and middle-income countries, and establishing tailored risk communication to directly address vaccine hesitancy. analysis.brief_en: A scoping review published on 8 November 2026 by Bioengineer.org identified critical data gaps in mpox vaccine effectiveness and implementation for pregnant women and children. The review, which completed its final database searches on 19 September 2025, found that vaccine effectiveness estimates were largely based on adult populations, with no specific data for these vulnerable groups. It noted significant implementation barriers, including supply limitations, cold-chain and logistical constraints, and vaccine hesitancy driven by safety concerns, especially during pregnancy. The review also highlighted the absence of randomised controlled clinical trials in pregnant women and children, as well as limited geographic representation from low- and middle-income countries. Despite these challenges, the authors identified key facilitators such as international coordination, targeted surveillance, and integration of immunisation into routine maternal and child health services. The review underscores the urgent need for prospective studies in these populations, equitable vaccine access, and tailored risk communication to address hesitancy.

news.content_zh: Bioengineer.org于2026年11月8日发表的一项范围综述揭示了猴痘 疫苗在孕妇和儿童群体中的关键数据缺口。该综述于2025年9月19日完成最终数据库检索,发现疫苗的效果估计主要基于成人人群,缺乏针对这些易感群体的特定数据。它指出实施过程中存在重大障碍,包括供应限制、冷链和物流约束,以及因安全顾虑而产生的疫苗接种犹豫,尤其是在妊娠期间。综述还强调了在孕妇和儿童中缺乏随机对照临床试验,以及来自低收入和中等收入国家的地理代表性不足。尽管面临这些挑战,作者识别出了一些关键促进因素,如国际合作、针对性的监测,以及将免疫接种纳入常规母婴健康服务。综述突显了在这些人群中进行前瞻性研究的迫切需求,实现疫苗的公平获取,并通过定制化风险沟通来应对接种犹豫。

Four mpox cases reported in Stanislaus County Staff reports Turlock Journal Published: Nov 4, 2026, 8:02 AM STANISLAUS COUNTY — Stanislaus County public health officials are urging residents to be aware of mpox symptoms and prevention measures after four recent cases of Clade I mpox were reported in the county. According to the Stanislaus County Health Services Agency, two of the cases have been confirmed as Clade I by the California Department of Public Health, while confirmatory testing is underway for the remaining two cases. Health officials said three of the individuals reported no recent international travel. The travel history of the fourth individual remains under investigation. Historically, Clade I mpox cases in the United States have been linked to international travel. However, public health officials said more cases have been identified among people without recent international travel since August 2026, suggesting the virus may now be spreading within U.S. communities. "While we have identified four cases in our county, we want residents to know that the risk to the general public remains low," said Dr. Thea Papasozomenos, Stanislaus County public health officer. "Being aware of the symptoms, getting vaccinated if at risk of exposure to mpox, and seeking medical care when needed are important ways to protect yourself and prevent the spread of mpox," Papasozomenos said. Mpox is a viral infection that can cause a painful or itchy rash and flu-like symptoms. Symptoms can include a rash or sores that resemble pimples or blisters, fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headaches, muscle aches and fatigue. Some people may develop only a few sores without other symptoms. Public health officials said the virus spreads primarily through close personal contact with an infected person, including skin-to-skin contact, intimate or sexual contact, contact with infected sores or bodily fluids, or contaminated items such as bedding, towels and clothing. Officials emphasized that mpox does not spread easily through casual contact, such as passing someone in a store or working in the same office. Most people recover within two to four weeks, although more serious illness can occur. The JYNNEOS vaccine is recommended for people at increased risk of exposure to mpox. The vaccine is administered in two doses approximately four weeks apart and helps protect against infection and severe illness. Residents experiencing an unexplained rash or sores are encouraged to contact a healthcare provider about testing. Health officials advise individuals who suspect they have mpox to avoid close physical contact with others, avoid sharing personal items and contact a healthcare provider before seeking in-person care. The Health Services Agency said it continues to work with the California Department of Public Health and local healthcare partners to monitor mpox activity and help prevent further spread of the virus. Four mpox cases reported in Stanislaus County Staff reports Turlock Journal Published: Nov 4, 2026, 8:02 AM STANISLAUS COUNTY — Stanislaus County public health officials are urging residents to be aware of mpox symptoms and prevention measures after four recent cases of Clade I mpox were reported in the county. According to the Stanislaus County Health Services Agency, two of the cases have been confirmed as Clade I by the California Department of Public Health, while confirmatory testing is underway for the remaining two cases. Health officials said three of the individuals reported no recent international travel. The travel history of the fourth individual remains under investigation. Historically, Clade I mpox cases in the United States have been linked to international travel. However, public health officials said more cases have been identified among people without recent international travel since August 2026, suggesting the virus may now be spreading within U.S. communities. "While we have identified four cases in our county, we want residents to know that the risk to the general public remains low," said Dr. Thea Papasozomenos, Stanislaus County public health officer. "Being aware of the symptoms, getting vaccinated if at risk of exposure to mpox, and seeking medical care when needed are important ways to protect yourself and prevent the spread of mpox," Papasozomenos said. Mpox is a viral infection that can cause a painful or itchy rash and flu-like symptoms. Symptoms can include a rash or sores that resemble pimples or blisters, fever, chills, swollen lymph nodes, headaches, muscle aches and fatigue. Some people may develop only a few sores without other symptoms. Public health officials said the virus spreads primarily through close personal contact with an infected person, including skin-to-skin contact, intimate or sexual contact, contact with infected sores or bodily fluids, or contaminated items such as bedding, towels and clothing. Officials emphasized that mpox does not spread easily through casual contact, such as passing someone in a store or working in the same office. Most people recover within two to four weeks, although more serious illness can occur. The JYNNEOS vaccine is recommended for people at increased risk of exposure to mpox. The vaccine is administered in two doses approximately four weeks apart and helps protect against infection and severe illness. Residents experiencing an unexplained rash or sores are encouraged to contact a healthcare provider about testing. Health officials advise individuals who suspect they have mpox to avoid close physical contact with others, avoid sharing personal items and contact a healthcare provider before seeking in-person care. The Health Services Agency said it continues to work with the California Department of Public Health and local healthcare partners to monitor mpox activity and help prevent further spread of the virus. PHOTO: THE NATION/ASIA NEWS NETWORK Published Nov 04, 2026, 12:15 PM Updated Nov 04, 2026, 01:08 PM Set as preferred source Listen Summarise Thailand recorded 470 mpox cases and three deaths from Jan 1 to Oct 31, 2026. The Department of Disease Control urged people with rashes, blisters or sores to seek medical help quickly. Officials said mpox needs PCR testing to confirm, as it can look like herpes or chickenpox. Most patients recover with supportive care, but pregnant women, young children and people with weak immunity face higher risk. The department told people to avoid close contact, sharing items and sexual activity with suspected cases. It also warned against stigma and said privacy and early care help reduce spread. AI generated BANGKOK – Thailand recorded 470 mpox cases and three deaths between Jan 1 and Oct 31, prompting its Department of Disease Control to urge people with suspicious symptoms to seek medical attention without delay. Montien Kanasawadse, director-general of the department, reported the figures on Nov 3, emphasising the importance of early diagnosis, continued disease surveillance and measures to prevent further transmission. He encouraged anyone who develops unusual rashes, blisters or sores, particularly after possible exposure to the virus, to consult a doctor and provide an accurate account of their symptoms and contact history. Mpox remains a communicable disease subject to surveillance under Thailand’s Communicable Diseases Act 2015 and the Thai Ministry of Public Health’s 2022 notification on diseases requiring surveillance. Mpox continues to spread internationally Montien noted that mpox transmission remains a concern in several regions worldwide. According to global figures cited by Thailand’s Department of Disease Control, 68,096 confirmed infections and 272 deaths were reported across 107 countries between Jan 1, 2025, and Aug 31. The department attributed these figures to a World Health Organization (WHO) report published on Sept 14. It stressed that the international figures cover a different reporting period from Thailand’s 2026 statistics. Early symptoms may be difficult to recognise Montien explained that mpox can affect anyone exposed to the virus, making awareness of its symptoms and transmission routes essential. Early signs commonly include fever, headaches, back pain, muscle aches and swollen lymph nodes. These may be followed by rashes or lesions on the skin, including the face, body, genitals and around the anus. Some patients develop only a few lesions, while others may experience pain around the anus. The skin changes can begin as raised red spots before developing into fluid-filled blisters, followed by pus-filled lesions and scabs. Crusting may begin in the centre of a lesion, and individual spots are often separate rather than clustered together. However, the department emphasised that symptoms do not always appear in the same order, and patients may not experience every characteristic sign of the infection. People should therefore seek medical advice if they notice unexplained rashes, blisters or sores, particularly following possible exposure, without waiting for the lesions to spread across their bodies. Montien also addressed concerns that may prevent patients from requesting medical assistance. More on this topic Thailand steps up mpox surveillance after two new cases Mpox can infect and replicate in the brain, US health researchers say in fatal HIV case Because lesions can appear in private areas of the body, some people may feel embarrassed or anxious about undergoing an examination. Montien stressed that illness should not be a source of shame and encouraged patients to discuss their symptoms and exposure history openly with medical professionals. Healthcare workers, he explained, would provide care with understanding while respecting patients’ privacy and maintaining confidentiality. PCR testing needed to confirm infection The Thai Department of Disease Control emphasised that mpox cannot be confirmed by examining a rash or photograph alone. Its symptoms can resemble those of herpes, chickenpox or other skin infections, making clinical assessment and laboratory testing necessary. Doctors consider patients’ symptoms and possible exposure history alongside laboratory findings. The principal method of confirmation is a polymerase chain reaction test, which detects the virus’s genetic material in samples collected from skin lesions. Routine blood tests cannot confirm mpox infection. Patients whose initial assessment is inconclusive, or whose tests are negative despite continuing symptoms, should return for further medical evaluation if additional lesions develop or their condition changes. They should also inform doctors of previous test results and treatment so that further examinations or repeat sampling can be considered when appropriate. Most patients recover with supportive care Direk Khampaen, deputy director-general of Thailand’s Department of Disease Control, said most people with mpox recover without requiring specialised treatment. Medical care generally focuses on managing symptoms, relieving pain, preventing secondary infections in skin lesions and reducing the risk of complications. However, people with weakened immune systems, pregnant women and young children face a greater risk of severe illness and require closer medical assessment. Doctors will determine whether additional treatment or admission to hospital is necessary according to each patient’s condition. Anyone experiencing severe pain, difficulty eating or drinking, lesions affecting the eyes or worsening symptoms should seek immediate medical attention. Patients urged to avoid close contact To reduce transmission, the department advised people to avoid direct contact with the skin or lesions of infected individuals. Close physical contact and sexual activity with anyone showing suspicious symptoms should also be avoided. Clothing, towels and bedding should not be shared, as contaminated objects can carry infectious material from bodily fluids or lesion scabs. Those awaiting medical assessment or test results should separate themselves from others, avoid sexual activity and close contact, and keep any lesions covered. They should also wash their hands regularly with soap or use 70% alcohol-based hand sanitiser and wear a well-fitting face mask. The department explained that not every confirmed mpox patient needs hospital admission. Doctors will assess the severity of symptoms, individual health risks and whether the patient can isolate safely at home. Patients recovering at home should avoid travelling, use separate eating utensils and personal belongings, and clean their clothing and other frequently used items. They must also follow medical advice and remain isolated until all lesions have healed, scabs have fallen off and new skin has formed. Lesions affecting mucous membranes must also have healed. Montien reiterated that prompt medical assessment can help patients receive appropriate care while reducing the likelihood of passing the infection to others. He also called on the public to avoid discrimination and stigma against people with mpox, stressing that respect for privacy is essential to ensuring equal access to healthcare. analysis.brief_en: Thailand has reported 470 cases of mpox and three deaths between January 1 and October 31, 2026, according to the Department of Disease Control. The outbreak has prompted public health officials to urge individuals experiencing rashes, blisters, or sores to seek medical attention promptly. Mpox symptoms can resemble those of herpes or chickenpox, necessitating PCR testing for confirmation. Most patients recover with supportive care, but vulnerable groups such as pregnant women, young children, and immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk. The department has advised avoiding close contact, sharing personal items, and sexual activity with suspected cases to prevent transmission. They also emphasized the importance of privacy and reducing stigma to encourage timely medical consultation. The outbreak is being monitored under Thailand’s Communicable Diseases Act 2015, and officials are focusing on early diagnosis, isolation, and public awareness to curb further spread.

news.content: Home News Peace Politics Health Humanitarian Business Programs Sports Podcasts LISTEN LIVE LATEST NEWS SSFF honours U-15 delegation after international football campaign in Azerbaijan Derik Cultural Festival organisers ask government to build theatre and public library in Juba Juba authorities review neighbourhood and market security operations Ateny says cultural exchange can break ethnic barriers and promote peace Derik Cultural Festival 2026 names Professor Peter Adwok Nyaba personality of the year OPINION: South Sudan needs leaders who listen, serve and deliver SSFF honours U-15 delegation after international football campaign in Azerbaijan Derik Cultural Festival organisers ask government to build theatre and public library in Juba Juba authorities review neighbourhood and market security operations Ateny says cultural exchange can break ethnic barriers and promote peace Derik Cultural Festival 2026 names Professor Peter Adwok Nyaba personality of the year OPINION: South Sudan needs leaders who listen, serve and deliver LISTEN LIVE Home › Health › Mpox cases rise in Western Equatoria Health Mpox cases rise in Western Equatoria Tricia Dominic • April 21, 2026 • 1 min read Mpox patient presenting rash symptoms - Courtesy Authorities in Western Equatoria State have confirmed a surge in Mpox infections, with 31 confirmed cases recorded between March and April as the outbreak spreads across multiple counties. State Minister of Information, James Abdallah, said the infections have been confirmed in different locations, with cases currently receiving treatment across the state health facilities. “These are the details. Number one is Yambio County with 14 positive cases tested in the national laboratory. Number two is Ezo with 13 positive cases... which made a total of 31 people tested positive cases. Then we have 102 suspected cases, which is still, we are waiting for the results,” Abdallah said. He added that samples from suspected cases have been sent to the National Public Health Laboratory under the Ministry of Health for confirmation. The minister also confirmed that no new deaths have been reported since the last recorded fatality in February. Health authorities say awareness campaigns are ongoing to help curb further transmission of the disease, which spreads through close contact with infected persons, contaminated materials, or animals. news.content_zh: 加利福尼亚州于2026年11月9日因猴痘暴发疫情宣布进入紧急状态,旨在加强该州的疫苗接种应对工作。该事件由IANS于2022年8月2日报道,强调了该病毒在州内的传播情况。猴痘暴发的出现促使采取紧急措施,表明其对公共卫生构成重大风险。然而,提供的证据并未具体说明病例数、死亡人数或接触人数。应对措施的重点是增强疫苗接种工作,但关于调查、检测或隔离措施的细节未被提供。该声明突显了当前形势的严重性,并强调了采取紧急行动以减轻猴痘病毒影响的必要性。
news.summary_zh: 加利福尼亚州于2026年11月9日因猴痘暴发疫情宣布进入紧急状态,旨在加强该州的疫苗接种应对工作。该事件由IANS于2022年8月2日报道,强调了该病毒在州内的传播情况。猴痘暴发的出现促使采取紧急措施,表明其对公共卫生构成重大风险。然而,提供的证据并未具体说明病例数、死亡人数或接触人数。应对措施的重点是增强疫苗接种工作,但关于调查、检测或隔离措施的细节未被提供。该声明突显了当前形势的严重性,并强调了采取紧急行动以减轻猴痘病毒影响的必要性。

supplementary_news.title: Review Identifies Critical Mpox Vaccine Data Gaps in Children and Pregnancy
supplementary_news.excerpt: A scoping review reveals third-generation mpox vaccines are recommended for pregnant women and children despite an absence of direct effectiveness data in these populations.

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 9, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Review Identifies Critical Mpox Vaccine Data Gaps in Children and Pregnancy by November 8, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 3 mins read 0 Review Identifies Critical Mpox Vaccine Data Gaps in Children and Pregnancy Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Although mpox poses disproportionate risks to pregnant women and children, clinical and observational evidence on immunisation and prevention in these vulnerable groups remains limited, according to a scoping review. The researchers mapped and synthesised existing published literature on vaccines as well as non-pharmaceutical preventive measures directed at mpox in pregnant women and paediatric populations. Their investigation aimed to assess reported vaccine effectiveness and to systematically identify the critical implementation barriers and facilitators influencing real-world prevention efforts across affected healthcare settings. To conduct the synthesis, the authors executed comprehensive searches across peer-reviewed and grey literature indexed in PubMed, Scopus, and Google for records published since 2008. The team completed their final database searches on 19 September 2025. Screening and data extraction followed a pre-specified review protocol structured in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews framework. Across the evaluated literature, forty-eight peer-reviewed articles and sixteen grey literature sources met the inclusion criteria, contributing evidence on immunisation strategies, preventive measures, documented effectiveness, implementation barriers, and delivery facilitators. Within the identified literature, third-generation non-replicating vaccines, including MVA-BN, JYNNEOS, Imvanex, and IMVAMUNE, were consistently recommended for use in pregnant women and children owing to their favourable safety profiles. However, the scoping review revealed that documented observational and programmatic estimates of vaccine effectiveness were derived almost entirely from adult study populations. Reported effectiveness stood at 36 to 86 percent for a single dose and reached up to approximately 89 percent following two doses. Crucially, the review identified no effectiveness estimate specific to pregnant women or children. The authors also found that no source reported vaccine use by pregnancy trimester, paediatric data remained restricted to small studies, and recommendations for ring vaccination and post-exposure prophylaxis were supported mainly by adult evidence. The review identified substantial implementation barriers that restrict mpox prevention and immunisation activities. Significant supply limitations and severe cold-chain and logistical constraints continue to impede vaccine rollout in low- and middle-income countries. In addition, vaccine hesitancy represents a major obstacle, largely driven by safety concerns that become particularly pronounced during pregnancy. These concerns are further intensified by the total absence of randomised controlled clinical trials conducted in pregnant women and paediatric groups. The authors also observed that geographic representation was severely skewed, noting that very few identified sources were centred on Africa or other low- and middle-income nations. Alongside these challenges, the scoping review documented key facilitators that have supported vaccination programs, such as international coordination, targeted surveillance initiatives, and the strategic integration of immunisation into routine maternal and child health services. The authors also highlighted flexible delivery strategies, specifically intradermal dosing, as mechanisms that can assist implementation under constrained resources. Looking ahead, the review outlined clear public health priorities, emphasising the urgent necessity of conducting prospective safety and immunogenicity studies in pregnancy and childhood, securing equitable vaccine access for low- and middle-income countries, and establishing tailored risk communication to directly address vaccine hesitancy. Subject of Research: Mpox immunisation and preventive measures in pregnant women and children Article Title: Immunisation and preventive measures against mpox in pregnant women and children: A scoping review Article References: Rahman, L., Eva, F. N., Ahsanuzzaman, A. K. M., Monami, S., Tabassum, A., Nabi, M. H., & Hawlader, M. D. H. (2026). Immunisation and preventive measures against mpox in pregnant women and children: A scoping review.
